messages.author: 37a92aff6efd2e3f
messages.subject: Stan model too many divergent transitions after warm up
parts:
Greetings,

I am a stan new user. Recently I have been trying to apply the hierarchical model (univariate changing settlement rate) in here: http://www.casact.org/pubs/forum/16wforum/Meyers.pdf on page 8.

The attached code shows where I am currently at with the model code. The current result I am seeing is either that the sampling takes 2 hours to run, with a handful of divergent transitions; or the sampling takes 5 minutes, but with a large number of divergent transitions. I am not sure if it's because of the prior distributions were misspecified or the modeling language was written incorrectly. Could someone please help me take a look at the script I have attached, which would produce a large amount of divergent transitions?


The code below is how I call the stan model in R:

initial_value <- function(){
  set.seed(12345)
  list(r_alpha = rnorm(13, 0, 1),
       r_beta = runif(13, -10, 0),
       a = rnorm(14, 0, 1),
       logelr = runif(1, -0.25, 0),
       gamma = rnorm(1, 0, 0.05),
       delta = rnorm(1, 0, 0.01))
}

CSR_dSO <- stan_model(file = "CSR_optimize.stan", model_name = "CSR_COLL")
CSR_samples <- sampling(CSR_dSO, seed = 12345, data = stan_data,
                        chains = 4, iter = 5000, warmup = 2000, thin = 2, cores = 2)

A side question: when should I use stan and when should I use stan_model + sampling?

Thank you,
Ethan Kang

messages.subject: Don't use hard constraints or uniform distributions
parts:
Hi, I think you should get rid of all these hard constraints and all these uniform priors.  Those are a disaster, for both computational and statistical reasons.  Also no need do things like sig = sqrt of something else, you can model sig directly.
A

to Stan-dev:  This model is a perfect example of where the verbose parser would be super helpful.

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: Don't use hard constraints or uniform distributions
parts:
Yeah, part of the problem is probably the uniform priors with hard constraints. But even if those are great priors in this situation you'd need to fix a few things to implement them correctly. If you have a parameter x and in the model block you write x ~ uniform(-10, 0) then x needs to be declared with <lower=-10,upper=0>. That is, the support of the parameter as declared in the parameters block should match the constraints implied by the density function used in the model block. Fixing that might help. But, like Andrew says, it's worth thinking about whether the uniforms with hard constraints are logically necessary. If not, then priors that decay smoothly are usually better. 

Hope that helps, 

Jonah

They're interchangeable. stan_model() gets around the need
to recompile the model every time. stan() should do that,
but all the kinks in that aren't worked out yet in RStan.
For example, just using stan() doesn't reuse the compiled
model in my installation on Mac OS X.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Don't use hard constraints or uniform distributions
parts:
We need to write up some Stan case studies to illustrate
the problems that arise.

The original BUGS default "diffuse" priors (like gamma(0.001, 0.001),
etc.) concentrate almost all of their prior mass away from 0.
That means if there's not much data, they will pull the
samples well away from 0 because the prior will dominate the
data. Andrew's written about this extensively in books and
papers.

The later BUGS default priors (uniform(0, 100), etc.) concentrate
all of their mass in that interval. The problem there is that
they essentially truncate. So what'll happen is that if there's
any mass near the boundary, what happens is that it gets truncated
and it moves the posterior mean away from the boundary. Consider
the case where the posterior would be something like normal(7, 2)
without the hard constraint and you add a (0, 10) constraint. Then
the posterior mean will be below 7 because you've truncated above 10
even though it's only 1.5 sd away from the posterior mean.

Neither of these assumptions is going to matter much if there's
a lot of data and the posterior is sharp and doesn't violate the
prior constraints. But that's not our usual operating conditions
with hierarchical models or other fine-grained statistical models.

- Bob

That is, the support of the parameter as declared in the parameters block should match the constraints implied by the density function used in the model block. Fixing that might help. data{
  // data is sorted by dev, then by accdate
  int<lower=0> N; // total number of rows (105 data points)
  int<lower=1, upper=14> accdate[N]; // accident date
  int<lower=1, upper=14> dev[N]; // development period
  real logloss[N]; // log of cumulative paid logloss
  real logep[14]; // earned premium of the acc years
}
parameters{
  real r_alpha[13];
  real r_beta[13];
  real logelr;
  real<lower=0> a[14];
  real gamma;
  real delta;
}
transformed parameters{
  real alpha[14];
  real beta[14];
  real speedup[14];

  alpha[1] <- 0; //AY parameter base level at first AY
  for (i in 2:14) alpha[i] <- r_alpha[i-1];
 
  for (i in 1:13) beta[i] <- r_beta[i];
  beta[14] <- 0;

  speedup[1] <- 1; //speedup parameter base level at first AY
  for (i in 2:14) speedup[i] <- speedup[i-1]*(1-gamma-(i-2)*delta);

}
model{
  real mu[N];
  real sig[N];

  //prior parameters
  r_alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
  r_beta ~ normal(-1, 0.5);
  gamma ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  delta ~ normal(0, 0.1);
  a ~ gamma(2, 2);  //a as sd of logloss
  logelr ~ normal(-1, 0.5);
 

  for (i in 1:N){
    mu[i] <- logep[accdate[i]]+logelr+alpha[accdate[i]]+beta[dev[i]]*speedup[accdate[i]];
    sig[i] <- a[dev[i]]; //assume each sig is a gamma distribution
  }

  //fit model to data
  logloss ~ normal(mu,sig);
}
